You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Assess the impact of Paul's mission in Ephesus.

(25 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** Ephesus was the chief city of the Roman province of Asia, a port and trading centre and the home of the great temple of Artemis (Diana). Paul's mission there, during his third missionary journey, lasted longer than in any other city, about two to three years (Acts 19:10; 20:31). Its impact may be assessed on the church, on the surrounding region, on the pagan religion and economy, and on Paul's own work.

**1. Impact on the believers.** Paul found some disciples who knew only the baptism of John. He baptised them in the name of the Lord Jesus, and when he laid his hands on them the Holy Spirit came on them and they spoke in tongues and prophesied (Acts 19:1-7). This brought them into full Christian life.

**2. Impact through teaching.** Paul spoke in the synagogue for three months, and when opposition arose he moved to the hall of Tyrannus, where he argued daily for two years (Acts 19:8-10). As a result, "all the residents of Asia, both Jews and Greeks, heard the word of the Lord" (Acts 19:10). The city became a base from which the Gospel spread through the province, which agrees with the traditions of churches at Colossae, Laodicea and elsewhere in Asia.

**3. Impact through miracles and exorcisms.** God did extraordinary miracles by Paul, so that handkerchiefs and aprons that had touched him healed the sick (Acts 19:11-12). The failure of the seven sons of Sceva, who tried to use the name of Jesus as a magic formula, caused fear and the name of the Lord Jesus was extolled (Acts 19:13-17).

**4. Impact on magic and superstition.** Many believers confessed their practices, and those who had practised magic burned their books publicly, to a value of fifty thousand pieces of silver (Acts 19:18-19). This marked a real break with the old way of life.

**5. Impact on the cult of Artemis and the local economy.** Demetrius, a silversmith who made silver shrines of Artemis, said that Paul had persuaded a great many people in Ephesus and in almost all of Asia that gods made with hands are not gods (Acts 19:23-27). The trade was threatened, and he stirred up a riot which filled the theatre with a shouting crowd. The town clerk calmed the people, observing that Paul and his companions had neither robbed temples nor blasphemed the goddess (Acts 19:35-41). The incident shows that the Gospel affected business and the civic religion, and also that Roman officials did not regard the Christians as criminals.

**6. Impact on Paul's ministry and writings.** Paul wrote 1 Corinthians from Ephesus (1 Corinthians 16:8), and the city later became an important centre of Christianity, and Paul's farewell address to the elders of Ephesus at Miletus (Acts 20:17-38) shows the depth of his relationship with the church. Paul says he faced many adversaries there (1 Corinthians 16:9).

**Conclusion.** The mission in Ephesus had a large and lasting impact. It produced a strong church, spread the Gospel across Asia, broke the grip of magic, challenged the cult of Artemis and showed the Roman world that Christianity was a growing force. It was one of the high points of Paul's career.
